explanation:
### What a ring buffer is

An array, and two numbers: where the oldest item is, and how many there are.
Nothing is ever moved. The circle is made by the modulo.

```cpp
bool RingBuffer::push(const Event& e) {
    if (full()) return false;
    slots_[(start_ + count_) % cap_] = e;   // one past the last, wrapped
    ++count_;
    return true;
}

bool RingBuffer::pop(Event& out) {
    if (empty()) return false;
    out = slots_[start_];
    start_ = (start_ + 1) % cap_;           // the next one along, wrapped
    --count_;
    return true;
}
```

`(start_ + count_) % cap_` is the slot just past the newest, which is exactly
where the next one goes; after `cap_` pushes it has come all the way round.

### Why the count, rather than a second index

The obvious alternative is `start_` and `end_`, and it has a famous problem:
when `start_ == end_` the buffer is either completely empty or completely
full, and the two are indistinguishable. The usual fixes are to keep a slot
permanently empty — paying one slot of capacity for a bit of information — or
to keep a flag. A count has neither problem and answers `size()` for free.

### Where the mistakes are

**A refused push that still changes something.** `push` has to return before
it touches anything. One of the hidden cases pushes into a full buffer twice
and then dumps, and a `start_` that moved on the way out shows up there.

**`at(i)` forgetting the start.** `slots_[i]` is right exactly until the first
wrap, which is why the sample passes and the hidden cases do not.

**`% cap_` with `cap_` of zero.** The capacity is at least 1, so this cannot
happen here; in code that takes a capacity from elsewhere it is the first
thing to check, because the modulo is undefined behaviour rather than a
crash you can rely on.

### Separate compilation

`ring_buffer.cpp` and `main.cpp` are compiled on their own and then linked.
The header is what they agree about: it is *included* into both, so both end
up with the same declarations, and each definition exists once. Get a
signature wrong in the `.cpp` and you do not get a compile error at all — you
get a link error, because what you defined is a different function from the
one that was declared.
